subject: physics_2
question_text: What is the phase difference between the incident and reflected waves when the wave is reflected by a rigid boundary?

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: at a rigid (fixed) boundary the displacement must stay zero, so the reflected wave is inverted relative to the incident wave — a phase change of π radian (180°). At a free boundary there is no phase change; the question asks only the rigid case.

recall_prompt: Say what happens to a wave at a rigid boundary, and the phase difference between the incident and reflected waves.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Wave inverted at the rigid end
lines: At a rigid boundary the end of the medium
cannot move, so the wave is reflected
inverted — a crest returns as a trough.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say the reflected wave is inverted, and why: the fixed end cannot move.
steps.why: The displacement at a fixed end must stay zero at every instant. Only an inverted reflected wave can cancel the incident wave there, so the inversion is forced by the boundary.
common_mistakes: Claiming the same inversion at a free boundary — a free end reflects with NO phase change.
Saying the wave loses energy at the boundary — an ideal rigid boundary reflects the full wave, only inverted.

recall.must_convey: That at a rigid boundary the reflected wave comes back inverted because the fixed end cannot move.
accept: a crest comes back as a trough
the fixed end must stay at zero displacement

steps.memory_tip: A fixed end cannot move, so the reflection must flip the wave to keep that point at zero.

steps.label: The phase difference
lines: An inverted wave is out of phase with the
incident wave by half a cycle.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write the value in radian — π — with the degree form beside it.
steps.why: Inversion means every point of the reflected wave is displaced opposite to the incident wave — exactly half a cycle apart, which in angle is π radian.
common_mistakes: Writing 2π — a full cycle brings a wave back in phase; the inversion is HALF a cycle, π.
Writing π/2 — a quarter cycle. The crest-to-trough flip is half a cycle.

recall.must_convey: That the phase difference between the incident and reflected waves is π radian, that is 180 degrees.
accept: half a cycle out of phase

steps.memory_tip: Flip = half a cycle = π. A full cycle 2π would mean no change at all.

insider_note: The value π carries the second mark, but examiners also look for the reason — the fixed end cannot move — before the number.
